headline: August Low Water Pins Bass and Blues to the Saybrook Rocks
subhead: With the river running warm and thin, the striper and bluefish game has shrunk down to the mouth, the dawn hours, and the breakwater riprap.
body_markdown:
By the first week of August the river tells you where to fish just by how it looks. The milfoil and water chestnut have choked out half the coves from Selden Creek down through Lord Cove, the ospreys off Great Island are flying young birds that dive-bomb the flats now instead of just the adults, and the current itself has gone soft and warm, the color of steeped tea from three weeks without real rain. This is the deep-summer river, and it fishes nothing like the river I was writing about in April. The shad are long gone up past Holyoke. What's left is a mouth-focused game, and it's been that way for two weeks running.

Here's the pattern I've watched play out for decades on this stretch, and it's holding true again this year: once the upper river warms into the high 70s and the weed growth locks up the coves, the striped bass and the bluefish both get pushed down to the one place that still has cold seams and moving water — the river mouth itself, from the Saybrook Breakwater out past the outer bar toward the Sound. The Sound side data backs up what I'm seeing on the water — Kings Point reading near 73 degrees, New London closer to 70 — and the river mouth sits right in that same range, warm enough that the fish don't want to sit in open water all day. They're holding tight to structure — the breakwater riprap, the rocks around the Nutmeg tower, the drop along Calves Island bar — and they're only really willing to feed hard in the low-light hours.

That's exactly the pattern we flagged a couple weeks back for this stretch of river — activity concentrating around dawn, dusk, and the tide changes — and it's still the whole ballgame. I had two mornings this week where the first hour of light, right on the last of the outgoing tide, produced striped bass to 28 inches on bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig right off the breakwater rocks, and then by 7:30 it was over. Dead. Sun gets up, water clears, fish drop back down into the deeper current seams and won't touch anything until the tide turns again or the light goes down. If you're used to all-day action from the spring run, this isn't that. This is get-there-before-sunrise fishing or plan on fishing after dark.

Bluefish have followed the bunker pods right into the mouth, same as they've been doing up and down the whole coast this summer with bait schools driving the bite everywhere from here to Raritan Bay. I watched a pod of peanut bunker get raided right off Great Island at first light Tuesday — birds working, blues blowing up on top, the kind of five-minute window where every cast on a small white Deceiver or a Kastmaster gets bit and then it's over as fast as it started. If you see the gulls diving off the flats or along the outer bar, don't wait — that bait won't sit still for long with blues under it.

At night, the bigger bass show up. I've had better luck the last ten days working eels — plain old live eels, no rig tricks needed — around the breakwater light and the rocks off the Lynde Point side, fished slow on the last two hours of the ebb when the current's still got some shoulder to it. That's where the better fish are, the 30-inch-plus class, and they want it slow and close to the bottom, not swimming fast through the water column. Bucktails still work if you don't want to mess with eels — white or chartreuse, an ounce and a half, bounced along the Calves Island bar edge on the same stage of tide.

The white perch bite has actually been the more dependable thing this week for anyone who wants a full bucket rather than a trophy. Whalebone Creek and the deeper holes up around the DEP Marina are holding decent numbers, and they'll eat grass shrimp or small bloodworm-tipped jigs after dark when the tide's moving, regardless of how brutal the daytime heat has been. It's not glamorous but it's honest fishing, and it's about the only thing in this river right now that isn't shut off by the sun.

Worth saying plainly — this has not been an easy week. Daytime fishing anywhere in the lower river has been mostly dead water, and I've had mornings where the window was so short I only got two fish to the boat before it shut off entirely. The Sound's heading into a neap tide around the 5th and 6th, which means the current through the mouth is going to soften up even more over the next several days. That's going to shrink the productive windows further, not widen them — expect the tide changes to matter more than ever, and I'd lean toward lighter bucktails and slower eel presentations to match the weaker flow. If I only had one shot this week, I'd take the last hour of the outgoing at first light off the breakwater, eel in hand, and I'd be packing up and gone before the sun cleared the trees at Old Lyme.
